entries.lesson_core_move: Test Fourier-integral convergence for continuous-time signals and LTI impulse responses to recognize when frequency-response analysis on the \(j\omega\) axis must be extended with Laplace-domain exponential weighting.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Limitations of the Fourier Transform
sections.learning_goal: Establish the recurring move for this lesson: students must test Fourier-integral convergence before treating a signal or impulse response as having a frequency response.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No symbolic graphics are needed; notation and formulas are sufficient.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Define the Fourier-transform convergence test as the first gate in the lesson: the core move is to decide whether $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t)e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$ is valid by checking integral convergence.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use $x(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$ as the minimal convergent example so the direct-instruction move remains concrete and minimal.
paragraph_plan: Open with the lesson-level map: convergence is the condition that determines if a Fourier frequency-response interpretation is lawful.
State the target operation as $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t)e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$ and the absolute-convergence check $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|x(t)|\,dt<\infty$.
Explain that this condition can pass for some signal classes and fail for nondecaying/growing classes, which creates the course motivation for Laplace weighting.

Preview the step sequence: first confirm a decaying case, then contrast with nondecaying and growing cases, then transfer the same test to impulse responses, then decide when $e^{-\sigma t}$ weighting is required.

sections.handoff_notes: No tutorial questions in this section. Keep this section purely direct-instruction and avoid inserting images or example-like walkthroughs.

sections.section_title: Testing Convergence for a Decaying Time Signal
sections.learning_goal: Show how to execute the core move on a convergent signal and conclude that Fourier analysis on $j\omega$ is valid.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No plots are needed; all judgments are from symbolic integral behavior.

question_policy.answer_format: five symbolic choices (true/false condition statements, expressions, or formulas)
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $x(t)=e^{-a|t|}$ with $a>0$, identify the correct statement about Fourier-transform convergence on $j\omega$.
distractor_plan: Pick wrong threshold assumptions such as requiring only boundedness, not absolute integrability.
Confuse bilateral with unilateral convergence and select a finite-slice conclusion.
Conclude growth in one side dominates regardless of decay elsewhere.
Claim exponential decay in one half-axis is always sufficient even when both sides diverge.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Demonstrate the one-step pattern for the example writer: evaluate the Fourier integral's absolute magnitude and compute finite bounds.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use the same base class as the tutorial, then specialize to $x(t)=e^{-2|t|}$.
paragraph_plan: Split the integral into two improper halves and show the envelope is $e^{-2|t|}$ after taking magnitude.
Evaluate both halves explicitly and reduce to geometric/exponential antiderivative values.
Conclude finite total area and mark the signal as having a valid $j\omega$-axis frequency response.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Test whether the Fourier transform converges for $x(t)=e^{-2|t|}$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Reach the conclusion that $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-2|t|}\,dt<\infty$, so $X(j\omega)$ exists.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Keep the same convergence rule but extend from a pure tutorial base case to a two-sided exponential envelope.
solution_step_plan: Take magnitude: $\left|e^{-2|t|}e^{-j\omega t}\right|=e^{-2|t|}$.
Split the absolute integral at $t=0$ into two one-sided improper integrals.
Evaluate both integrals to finite values and sum them.
State that absolute convergence implies the Fourier integral is well-defined.
practice_variation_axes: Change decay rate from 2 to a general $a>0$ and reuse the same pattern.
Swap between two-sided and one-sided decaying forms.
Ask for the same move on complex sinusoids multiplied by a decaying envelope.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep worked example symbolic and concise; use practice that mirrors the same absolute-integral workflow.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Divergence for a Nondecaying Time Signal
sections.learning_goal: Apply the same move to a nondecaying signal and diagnose exactly why convergence fails on the $j\omega$ axis.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image is needed; divergence is inferred from symbolic magnitude growth.

question_policy.answer_format: five symbolic choices (expressions and condition statements)
question_policy.practice_question_model: For $x(t)=1$, which option correctly describes whether a frequency-response $X(j\omega)$ exists?
distractor_plan: Choose a finite interval argument and ignore the infinite support.
Claim oscillation of $e^{-j\omega t}$ guarantees convergence by cancellation for all signals.
Use boundedness of $x(t)$ as the only criterion.
Conclude convergence exists only when $\omega\neq 0$.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Demonstrate one-way and two-sided nonconvergence with an explicit divergent absolute-value integral.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use the nondecaying template $x(t)=1$.
paragraph_plan: Rewrite the magnitude integral for a nondecaying signal and test it directly.
Show the resulting improper integral has infinite area.
Label this as a fail for Fourier-transform existence on the $j\omega$ axis.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Test convergence for $x(t)=1$ and decide if a Fourier transform exists.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show the absolute integral is infinite and therefore conclude no $X(j\omega)$ in the ordinary Fourier sense.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Change the tested signal from decaying to constant to isolate the failure of convergence.
solution_step_plan: Write $\left|1\cdot e^{-j\omega t}\right|=1$.
Compute $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}1\,dt$ and classify it as divergent.
State clearly that divergence fails the lesson core move.
Record the implication: frequency-response language is not justified without extension.
practice_variation_axes: Replace $1$ with another nondecaying bounded signal (e.g., shifted rectangular pulse with infinite support).
Test statements about endpoint behavior versus whole-domain integrability.
Vary whether the signal is even, odd, or shifted while keeping nondecay.

sections.handoff_notes: Make the failure explicit and binary: this example should be the first clear 'does not converge' anchor for learners.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Divergence for a Growing Exponential Signal
sections.learning_goal: Use the core move on a growing signal to confirm that exponential increase forces divergence in the Fourier framework.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; growth rate logic is captured algebraically.

question_policy.answer_format: five symbolic choices (conditions on exponent sign/rates and resulting transform validity)
question_policy.practice_question_model: For $x(t)=e^{2t}u(t)$, choose the correct conclusion about Fourier convergence and the next step the learner should take.
distractor_plan: Pick bounded-oscillation from $e^{-j\omega t}$ as sufficient even when amplitude grows.
Claim causal support guarantees Fourier existence regardless of growth rate.
Assume the one-sided integral converges because $\omega \neq 0$.
State that any exponential can be normalized by phase rotation and therefore converges.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Model the same absolute-integral test now with a growth exponent to show where and why divergence appears.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use $x(t)=e^{2t}u(t)$ as the minimal growing-causal counterexample.
paragraph_plan: Write the absolute-value Fourier integral and simplify to a one-sided exponential growth integral.
Evaluate the improper upper-limit behavior and show it diverges.
Map this result to the lesson rule: the signal violates the prerequisite for ordinary Fourier frequency-response analysis.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Test whether the Fourier transform converges for $x(t)=e^{2t}u(t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Conclude that the one-sided absolute integral diverges and therefore no standard Fourier transform exists.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Hold the same integral template but move from nondecay to exponential growth to create a stronger divergence pattern.
solution_step_plan: Apply the magnitude and one-sided support: $\left|e^{2t}u(t)e^{-j\omega t}\right|=e^{2t}u(t)$.
Compute the improper integral over $[0,\infty)$.
Show the antiderivative grows unbounded as upper limit $\to \infty$.
Conclude divergence and pass forward to weighted-form remediation.
practice_variation_axes: Vary the growth parameter $a$ in $e^{at}u(t)$ and classify convergence by sign.
Ask causal versus anti-causal growth cases.
Ask the same skill on a shifted growth signal $e^{a(t-t_0)}u(t-t_0)$.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this step clearly distinct from nondecaying failure: growth rate is the key diagnostic.

sections.section_title: Testing Whether an Impulse Response Has a Frequency Response
sections.learning_goal: Transfer the core move to LTI impulse responses and decide convergence for $h(t)$ exactly as for signals.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No circuit or waveform visuals required for this step.

question_policy.answer_format: five symbolic choices (classification of impulse responses by convergence outcome)
question_policy.practice_question_model: Which signal has a valid frequency response from the list: $h(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$, $h(t)=\frac{1}{1+t}u(t)$, or $h(t)=e^{2t}u(t)$?
distractor_plan: Classify based on sign pattern of $h(t)$ rather than integrability.
Treat one-sided decay as sufficient without checking the full impulse-response integral.
Apply signal-only intuition and miss the analogous test for $h(t)$ in system context.
Conclude frequency-response existence whenever a Laplace expression can be written.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Reinforce that convergence testing is identical for impulse responses: verify $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|h(t)|dt$ before assigning frequency-response status.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Anchor with a stable impulse response such as $h(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$.
paragraph_plan: State the same test now in system language: $H(j\omega)$ exists only if $h(t)$ is absolutely integrable.
Walk through one convergent and one nonconvergent candidate shape.
Close with the branch rule: convergent $h(t)$ keeps Fourier frequency response; nonconvergent $h(t)$ does not.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Test whether $h(t)=\frac{1}{1+t}u(t)$ has a Fourier-domain frequency response.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show divergence of $\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{1+t}\,dt$ and conclude no finite $H(j\omega)$ in the Fourier sense.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Shift the object under test from $x(t)$ to $h(t)$ while preserving the same absolute-convergence grammar.
solution_step_plan: Insert $h(t)=\frac{1}{1+t}u(t)$ into $\left|\int h(t)e^{-j\omega t}dt\right|\le \int |h(t)|dt$.
Reduce to $\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{1+t}dt$ and evaluate divergence.
State nonexistence of $H(j\omega)$ under Fourier assumptions.
Prepare transition language: this is the exact point where weighted (Laplace) thinking becomes necessary.
practice_variation_axes: Replace with another marginally decaying/nondecaying impulse response family.
Ask causal vs anti-causal impulse responses with the same tail behavior.
Add a stable convergent comparison case to contrast with divergence.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the step tied to system intuition without adding transfer-function derivations or pole-zero plots.

sections.section_title: Deciding When Laplace-Domain Weighting Is Needed
sections.learning_goal: Use the convergence outcomes above to decide when Fourier analysis must be extended with an exponential weight $e^{-\sigma t}$.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; transition to Laplace-domain weighting is derived symbolically.

question_policy.answer_format: five symbolic choices (correct condition on $\sigma$ and remedy choice)
question_policy.practice_question_model: For $x(t)=e^{at}u(t)$ with $a>0$, which statement is correct?
distractor_plan: Choosing any nonzero $\sigma$ is treated as a remedy without checking sign constraints.
Assuming Fourier convergence from Laplace existence on some $s$ automatically implies a Fourier transform.
Using $\sigma=0$ by default regardless of growth sign.
Ignoring causal/anti-causal direction when selecting the required inequality on $\sigma$.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show the exact remedy decision: if divergence is from growth, test whether $e^{-\sigma t}x(t)$ can be absolutely integrable for some $\sigma$.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use $x(t)=e^{2t}u(t)$ as a base failure and recover the needed inequality for $\sigma$.
paragraph_plan: Restate the fail cases from prior steps and identify the specific growth term driving failure.
Introduce weighted integral $\int x(t)e^{-\sigma t}e^{-j\omega t}dt$ as a controllable extension.
State the decision rule: choose $\sigma$ so the weighted magnitude is absolutely integrable, then move to $X(s)$ language.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For $x(t)=e^{2t}u(t)$, decide whether Fourier or weighted Laplace-domain analysis applies and find the condition on $\sigma$ that would permit convergence.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show Fourier fails, then derive $\sigma>2$ from the weighted integral and conclude that weighted analysis on the $s$-plane, not the $j\omega$ axis, is the valid next representation.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This final step is a controlled extension that adds the minimal extra parameter $\sigma$ to remedy the previously demonstrated growth-divergence case.
solution_step_plan: State the weighted form and rewrite the magnitude integral as $\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{(2-\sigma)t}\,dt$.
Solve the convergence inequality on the exponent and derive the required bound for $\sigma$.
Contrast with $\sigma=0$ to show why Fourier alone failed.
Conclude the branch rule for the lesson: use Fourier when the unweighted integral converges; otherwise introduce Laplace-domain weighting.
practice_variation_axes: Generalize from $e^{2t}u(t)$ to $e^{at}u(t)$ and solve for the required $\sigma$.
Swap causal support direction and test whether the sign inequality flips.
Apply the same decision step to mixed exponentials like $te^{at}u(t)$ with required comparison.

sections.handoff_notes: This section should end with explicit transfer guidance to the next lesson topic: when and why the $j\omega$ slice is insufficient.

entries.lesson_title: Signals Whose Fourier Transform Does Not Converge
entries.lesson_core_move: Determine whether a continuous-time signal lacks a convergent Fourier transform by testing the Fourier-transform integral for convergence and interpreting nondecaying or growing behavior as requiring Laplace-domain exponential weighting.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Signals Whose Fourier Transform Does Not Converge
sections.learning_goal: Establish the standard Fourier-transform setup and show that convergence is decided by the magnitude of the signal on each unbounded support interval.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; all reasoning is symbolic integral evaluation.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed because the step is algebraic and scalar.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Not applicable for tutorial section.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Introduce the Fourier-transform definition and a practical convergence screen: test improper integrals and classify limits at $t\to\pm\infty$ before symbolic computation.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use $X(j\omega)=\int_0^{\infty}e^{-at}e^{-j\omega t}dt$ with $a>0$ as the convergent baseline.
paragraph_plan: State $X(j\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(t)e^{-j\omega t}dt$ and emphasize that $|e^{-j\omega t}|=1$, so magnitude behavior comes from $x(t)$.
Show the absolute-value test form on each side of the support and connect it to improper-integral growth rules.
Work through a convergent decaying exponential and contrast with a constant/tiny-frequency test signal that does not dampen.
Summarize that nondecaying or growing signals are the trigger for the upcoming Laplace weighting move.

example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Not applicable for tutorial section.

sections.section_title: Testing Fourier-Transform Integral Convergence
sections.learning_goal: Apply the convergence criterion to a convergent benchmark and check integral setup for one-sided signals.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; classify using closed-form integral behavior.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed because all tasks are symbolic.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Determine whether the Fourier-transform integral converges for $x(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$.
distractor_plan: Include a choice that uses oscillation to incorrectly conclude divergence despite exponential decay.
Include a choice that swaps the support side and checks only $t<0$.
Include a choice that forgets that $|e^{-j\omega t}|=1$.
Include a choice that assumes boundary terms always converge when the exponent is nonnegative.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Test convergence of $X(j\omega)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-2t}e^{-j\omega t}dt$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show the integral has finite magnitude and therefore a convergent Fourier-transform form under standard conditions.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This step turns the tutorial rule into one concrete worked example using a stable, decaying template.
solution_step_plan: Write the one-sided integral explicitly over the support.
Replace the complex kernel by magnitude: $|e^{-2t}e^{-j\omega t}|=e^{-2t}$.
Evaluate the improper integral and verify it is finite.
Record the verdict as convergent and the reason in one sentence.
practice_variation_axes: Change the decay constant from $2$ to a parameter $a$ and classify signs.
Replace with a shifted support, e.g., $u(t-1)$.

sections.handoff_notes: For this example, keep arithmetic short and directly connect each line to the convergence decision.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Nondecaying Signals That Do Not Converge
sections.learning_goal: Use the same procedure to classify nondecaying signals as Fourier-nonconvergent on unbounded intervals.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; use constant and periodic forms in formulas only.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: No images required.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Classify whether $x(t)=1$ has a convergent Fourier transform.
distractor_plan: Include a distractor that says boundedness alone implies convergence.
Include a distractor that uses only one-tail analysis and misses divergence on the other tail.
Include a distractor that confuses distributional/engineered conventions with standard improper-integral convergence.
Include a distractor that treats periodic terms as always convergent.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Determine convergence for $x(t)=\cos(\omega_0 t)$ over $(-\infty,\infty)$ using magnitude bounds.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Conclude nonconvergence in the standard Fourier integral sense due to non-decay on unbounded support.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Extend testing from strictly constant signals to bounded periodic signals to reinforce the divergence pattern.
solution_step_plan: Express the Fourier integral and confirm support is unbounded.
Take magnitudes to show the integrand does not decay in time.
Argue that the integral over an unbounded interval diverges.
Name the next diagnostic: growing signals are the opposite extreme and also fail.
practice_variation_axes: Replace with a DC-shifted version, e.g., $1+0.1\cos(\omega_0 t)$.
Restrict to $t\ge 0$ and compare the convergence verdict.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this step focused on nondecaying tails; avoid any exponential-weighted form here.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Growing Signals That Do Not Converge
sections.learning_goal: Classify explicit growing one-sided exponentials as Fourier-nonconvergent by side-of-growth checks.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; classify with one-sided exponential growth inequalities.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: No images needed.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Classify convergence of $x(t)=e^{3t}u(t)$ in Fourier-transform form.
distractor_plan: Include an option that assumes oscillation dominates and hides unbounded growth.
Include an option that incorrectly applies the decaying example inequality $a>0$ unchanged.
Include an option that gives convergence without stating any inequality on exponent sign.
Include an option that moves the support to $t<0$ without adjusting the conclusion.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Test convergence of $x(t)=e^{3t}u(t)$ by evaluating the implied weighted-free magnitude integral.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show divergence because $\int_0^{\infty}e^{3t}dt$ is unbounded.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Apply the same convergence test to growth instead of nondecaying constants to isolate the second failure mode.
solution_step_plan: Write the Fourier integral on $[0,\infty)$.
Take magnitudes and remove the unit-magnitude kernel.
Recognize $\int_0^{\infty}e^{3t}dt$ does not converge.
Mark this as a growth-induced failure case that motivates exponential damping.
practice_variation_axes: Move from $e^{3t}$ to $e^{-3t}$ and ask if convergence flips.
Add finite-duration truncation as a boundary-control variation.

sections.handoff_notes: Use this section as explicit contrast: same test, different tail behavior, same conclusion of nonconvergence.

sections.section_title: Identifying Signals That Need Exponential Weighting
sections.learning_goal: Decide when multiplication by $e^{-\sigma t}$ can restore convergence and state the required real-condition direction.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; all diagnostics stay in symbolic exponent arithmetic.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: No images needed.

question_policy.practice_question_model: For $x(t)=e^{2t}u(t)$, what condition on $\sigma$ makes $\int_0^{\infty}e^{(2-\sigma)t}dt$ finite?
distractor_plan: Include a distractor that uses $\sigma<2$ as the convergent condition.
Include a distractor that omits one-sided support and applies a symmetric inequality.
Include a distractor that uses non-strict inequality at equality by mistake.
Include a distractor that sets the condition on $\omega$ instead of $\sigma$.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Find the condition on $\sigma$ for $x(t)=e^{2t}u(t)$ so that $\int_0^{\infty}e^{(2-\sigma)t}dt$ converges.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that convergence requires $\sigma>2$, matching a negative net exponent after weighting.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Bridge the prior failure case to the first corrective technique by adding a single real exponential factor.
solution_step_plan: Substitute the weighted signal into the Fourier integral form.
Reduce to the scalar criterion $\int_0^{\infty}e^{(2-\sigma)t}dt$.
Apply the standard condition for improper exponentials to derive $\sigma>2$.
Phrase the result as the signal-specific threshold for later $s=\sigma+j\omega$ work.
practice_variation_axes: Generalize to $e^{at}u(t)$ and identify condition $\sigma>a$.
Use two-sided growth templates and require combined constraints.

sections.handoff_notes: This section should explicitly hand off the reason for Laplace-domain damping and not solve any $s$-plane geometry yet.

entries.lesson_core_move: Apply exponential weighting to a continuous-time signal to determine how multiplying by \(e^{-\sigma t}\) can make a nonconvergent Fourier-transform integral converge and motivate the Laplace-domain variable \(s=\sigma+j\omega\).

sections.section_title: Introduction to Exponential Weighting
sections.learning_goal: Introduce why multiplying by a damping term can restore convergence of a Fourier-transform integral and motivate the Laplace-domain real-part parameter.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed. The step is driven by algebraic notation and convergence conditions.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use pure symbolic scaffolding and avoid any plot or diagram.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show that adding a damping factor creates a controllable decay via $e^{-\sigma t}$ and motivates the Laplace-domain real-part parameter.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with $x(t)=u(t)$ and contrast $\int_0^{\infty}u(t)e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$ with $\int_0^{\infty}u(t)e^{-\sigma t}e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$.
paragraph_plan: State the concrete learning target: use one damping factor to repair divergent Fourier behavior.
Review the raw Fourier-transform form and explain why non-decaying right-sided signals can fail the convergence test.
Introduce the weighted signal $x_w(t)=x(t)e^{-\sigma t}$ and interpret $\sigma$ as a tunable real damping factor for $t>0$.
Work the base case with $x(t)=u(t)$, showing that $e^{-\sigma t}$ creates a convergent integral only when the real decay is positive.
Preview the remaining steps: apply this weighting to additional signals, test convergence thresholds, then rewrite with $s=\sigma+j\omega$.

sections.handoff_notes: Do not ask practice questions in this step. Keep it short and symbolic to reduce cognitive load before example phases.

sections.section_title: Applying a Decaying Weight to a Nondecaying Signal
sections.learning_goal: Apply exponential weighting to a right-sided nondecaying signal and compute the resulting convergence condition.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed. All decisions come from one-dimensional exponent inequalities and algebra.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: No signal plots. Keep to symbolic expressions and inequalities.

question_policy.practice_question_model: For $x(t)=u(t)$, test convergence of $\int_0^{\infty}x(t)e^{-\sigma t}e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$. Which condition on $\sigma$ is correct and what is the transformed form when it holds?
distractor_plan: Include a distractor that ignores the sign of $\sigma$ and claims no restriction is needed.
Include a distractor that puts $\sigma<0$ as the convergence condition.
Include a distractor that incorrectly treats $\omega$ as affecting convergence.
Include a distractor that uses the wrong final denominator sign.
Include a distractor that forgets one-sided support and assumes two-sided divergence in every case.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Evaluate $\int_0^{\infty}u(t)e^{-\sigma t}e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$ and state the condition on $\sigma$ for convergence.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show the weighted integrand becomes $e^{-(\sigma+j\omega)t}$ and derive $\sigma>0$, with result $\frac{1}{\sigma+j\omega}$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first concrete worked example of the tutorial idea using the minimum nondecaying right-sided signal.
solution_step_plan: Write the weighted transform integral for $x(t)=u(t)$.
Combine exponent terms into one kernel $e^{-(\sigma+j\omega)t}$.
Apply one-sided exponential convergence with real part criterion $\sigma>0$.
Integrate and simplify the result to a closed form.
Separate the valid condition from the symbolic transformed value.
practice_variation_axes: Swap support to $u(-t)$ and preserve the same weighting idea.
Replace $\sigma$ by a parameter and ask for the required inequality on that parameter.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the example strictly symbolic. Focus on exponent combination and the real-part convergence check.

sections.section_title: Testing Convergence After Weighting
sections.learning_goal: Test convergence when the signal is already decaying and verify how inherent decay and weighting combine.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed. Use symbolic comparison against the integrated exponent’s real part.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: No visual stimuli requested.

question_policy.practice_question_model: For $x(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$, determine the condition for convergence of $\int_0^{\infty}e^{-2t}e^{-\sigma t}e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$.
distractor_plan: Include a distractor that adds decay rates as $\sigma-2$ instead of $\sigma+2$.
Include a distractor that constrains $\omega$ and ignores the real-part rule.
Include a distractor that claims the integral always diverges.
Include a distractor that uses $\sigma<-2$.
Include a distractor with right convergence inequality but wrong final expression denominator.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Test convergence of $\int_0^{\infty}e^{-2t}e^{-\sigma t}e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$ and derive the inequality on $\sigma$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show the exponent is $-(\sigma+2+j\omega)t$, so convergence requires $\sigma>-2$, then provide the simplified integral result.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds intrinsic signal decay to the same weighted integral pattern, so exponent combination must account for both rates.
solution_step_plan: Substitute $x(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$ in the weighted expression.
Collapse exponents into real-imaginary components.
Apply the convergence rule from the real exponent part.
Compute the resulting symbolic integral and final expression.
Reinforce that $\omega$ changes oscillation only.
practice_variation_axes: Replace $2$ with a positive parameter $a$ and keep the same process.
Shift the one-sided support and verify the method remains the same.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the one-sided support clear. The key is adding exponents correctly and interpreting decay from the real part.

sections.section_title: Choosing a Larger Weight for a Growing Signal
sections.learning_goal: Find the minimum damping level needed for an exponentially growing signal to become convergent under weighting.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed. All work is algebraic with inequality constraints.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use strict symbolic parameter checks; no graphing required.

question_policy.practice_question_model: For $x(t)=e^{2t}u(t)$, determine the least $\sigma$ needed for $\int_0^{\infty}e^{2t}e^{-\sigma t}e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$ to converge.
distractor_plan: Include a distractor that gives $\sigma<2$.
Include a distractor that allows equality $\sigma\le2$ as sufficient.
Include a distractor that uses a two-sided convergence test instead of one-sided support.
Include a distractor that keeps $j\omega$ in the inequality.
Include a distractor with an incorrect sign in the final closed form.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Find the condition on $\sigma$ for $\int_0^{\infty}e^{2t}e^{-\sigma t}e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$ to converge, and simplify the result.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Combine exponents as $e^{(2-\sigma-j\omega)t}$, derive $\sigma>2$, and produce the symbolic transform form.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Region of Convergence
sections.learning_goal: Define the region of convergence for a Laplace transform as the set of $s$ values where the exponentially weighted integral is finite.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No visual required for first introduction; keep this section fully symbolic with inequalities and integral conditions.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Help the writer define the ROC from the convergence condition of $X(s)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(t)e^{-st}\,dt$ and interpret ROC as a subset of the $s$-plane.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with a single-sided exponential example, such as $x(t)=e^{-at}u(t)$, where ROC is immediately testable from a one-integral inequality.
paragraph_plan: Introduce the weighted Laplace-integral form $X(s)=\int x(t)e^{-\sigma t}e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$ and define what it means for the transform to exist at one $s$ value.
Show the direct link between convergence and a real-part condition by isolating the exponential decay/growth term $e^{-\sigma t}$ from $e^{-j\omega t}$.
Explain that the ROC is the complete set of $\sigma$ (equivalently $s$ points) that satisfy the corresponding inequality and therefore all make the integral finite.
Conclude by previewing that later sections convert point tests into inequalities and then geometric regions in the $s$-plane.
